extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and students of U.S. patent law (inventors, patent attorneys, judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules for determining whether a claimed subject-matter constitutes an 'invention' and whether it is 'novel' under U.S. patent law, including evidentiary indicia (commercial success, prior art, inventorship, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention in combination of old elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When an old thing is combined with other things in a new organization, invention may be present in the combination though absent from the separate parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination of known elements can be patentable if the new organization produces a new result or mode of operation (Telephone Cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success / general use as evidence of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If a process or machine has gone into general use and has displaced formerly employed analogous processes or things, that fact is sufficient to turn the scale in favor of the existence of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may properly instruct juries that general adoption and displacement of prior devices is sufficient evidence of invention absent evidence showing the success was due to some other cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on weight of commercial success evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success or extensive sale does not necessarily prove invention when the success is due to advertising, business energy, cheaper manufacture, or because the patented feature is only a part of a complete device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is often offset by proof that the marketplace success derived from non-inventive causes (e.g., vigorous advertising, lower cost of manufacture, or the patent covering only a subpart of a popular product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Success after others failed as evidence of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee's success in achieving a result after others seeking the same result have failed is a strong circumstance establishing the quality of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative evidence that others attempted and failed to solve the problem supports a finding of invention (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acquiescence as indicia of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Public acquiescence in the inventor's rights over an extended period is a strong circumstance to prove invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longstanding acceptance of the inventor's exclusive rights (e.g., no competing claims or challenges over time) supports inventive character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of form vs change of operation/function/result
rubrics_metrics.description: To change the form of a machine or manufacture is sometimes invention and sometimes not; changes within mere construction are not invention, but changes that involve a new mode of operation, function, or result are invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the modification affects operation or result rather than mere shape or construction; if it does, it may be inventive unless excluded by other legal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in proportions: mechanical vs chemical
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the proportions of a machine or manufacture will seldom amount to invention; but changing proportions of ingredients of a chemical composition may be invention when it produces an entirely distinct article with distinct mode of operation and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Goodyear's soft vs hard vulcanized rubber — proportion changes produced distinct, patentable products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of invention is a question of fact; high threshold to invalidate
rubrics_metrics.description: A question of invention is a question of fact to be determined by legal rules; patents are not held void for want of invention except where invention is clearly absent, and invention is not clearly absent unless the subject was logically deducible from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require clear absence of invention before invalidating a patent; borderline cases are resolved in favor of patent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art sources and confidentiality of patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Every inventor is presumed to have borrowed from another whatever was actually first invented or used by another, or previously patented or described in a printed publication; but a mere (unissued) application is confidential and not part of the public prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior patents and printed publications are record evidence of prior art; unpublished/secret patent applications do not generally count as prior art unless their contents become public in a manner recognized by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship and entitlement to patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can be granted only to those who invented the inventions they cover, or to assignees or legal representatives of those inventors; the patent must disclose the real inventor and be founded on his right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent issued to a non-inventor (except by valid assignment) is invalid; proper naming/disclosure of inventors is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole inventor vs joint inventor: conception and embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: If one person conceives the plan of a machine and embodies it without assistance, he is a sole inventor; where two or more persons exercise inventive faculties in mutual production, they are joint inventors regardless of who constructed the first specimen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventorship turns on contribution to inventive conception, not necessarily who physically built or first practiced the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction alone does not confer inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: If one person does all the inventing and another only the constructing, the inventor (not the constructor) is the sole inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical or labor skills used to embody a conceived invention do not by themselves make the mechanic an inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor practical contributions can create joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one joint inventor conceived the main idea, another who makes practical suggestions of value that assist in working out the main idea or contributes an independent part helping to create the whole is a joint inventor, even if his contribution is of minor importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the collaborator contributed an inventive part or practical, inventive suggestions; mere minor or negligible suggestions may not suffice; if the contribution is claimed separately in the patent, that person may not be a joint inventor of the joint claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere suggestion or imparting general knowledge does not make joint inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who only furnish a fund of general knowledge, give isolated points of information during experiments, or offer mere suggestions are not thereby made joint inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General background knowledge, consulting, or isolated advice during development ordinarily does not create inventorship rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception without enabling embodiment can still be inventorship, but not mere delegation to execute
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who furnishes all the ideas needed to produce the invention may be the sole inventor even if he lacks skill to make a model or drawing and employs others to embody it; however, merely conceiving a result and then employing another to produce it is not invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine inventive conception (patentable) and mere delegation of routine implementation (not an invention by the delegator alone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment timing and patent validity regarding joint inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application has been assigned prior to issuance, a patent granted to the assignee may avoid the invalidity that would otherwise follow from failure to name joint inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments and their timing can affect challenges based on inventorship; statutory and equitable nuances apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint patent including a non-inventor or claiming independent inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint patent obtained by several persons for what was actually invented solely by one of them is void; likewise where a joint patent includes separate claims covering independent inventions made by different applicants (a claim covering the invention made solely by one applicant is void).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require convincing evidence to invalidate a patent on this ground; separate, independent inventions should not be improperly combined in a joint patent without proper inventorship/assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of novelty / anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'anticipate' an invention (negate novelty) it is necessary that all of the elements of the invention or their equivalents be found in one single description or structure where they do substantially the same work in substantially the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires a single prior reference (or structure) disclosing substantially the same combination/means performing the same function in the same way; piecemeal combination of references is not anticipation (but may be obviousness-related).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign prior knowledge/use generally does not negate novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is not negatived by prior knowledge or prior use in a foreign country of the subject of a U.S. patent, provided the subject had nowhere been patented to another and nowhere described in a printed publication when it was invented by the U.S. applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign uses that were not publicly patented or printed at the relevant time do not defeat U.S. novelty; statutory provisions distinguish these situations (Revised Statutes cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of domestic knowledge of foreign use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge possessed in the United States by someone else that a subject was known and used in a foreign country before its invention here is not such domestic knowledge as will negative novelty, unless the U.S. applicant learned of that disclosure before his date of conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant's own ignorance of the foreign prior use does not defeat novelty unless the applicant actually learned of the disclosure before conceiving the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of other patents and foreign patents on novelty (timing rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is not negatived by a U.S. patent issued after the contested invention was made (even if applied for earlier), nor by a prior private foreign patent, and not by a public English patent unless sealed before the American's invention; conversely, certain foreign patents (e.g., French when sealed/enrolled; German upon publication) can negative novelty as of their effective/published date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country-specific timing rules determine whether a foreign patent/publication can be prior art; an application's filing date or issuance date may have different effects for anticipation vs priority of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office applications as prior art / proof of date
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere application in the Patent Office is confidential and is not of itself part of the prior art to anticipate another patent, though it may be sufficient to prove a date of invention; however, if an application was filed before the contested invention and its specification/drawings fully disclose the subject and there had been actual prior use, that application may negative novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between confidential pending applications (not public prior art) and earlier-filed applications whose disclosures and evidence of use are admissible on issues of priority/anticipation under particular circumstances.
